chiengora.types: Chiengora has no formal grades; spinners sort it by breed, coat type and how cleanly the undercoat was separated. Double-coated breeds with long, dense undercoats, such as Samoyed, Siberian Husky, Great Pyrenees and Newfoundland, give the most spinnable fiber, while short, stiff single coats are generally unsuitable. An academic comparison of five breeds found similar chemistry but large differences in diameter and linear density, with only Lhasa Apso and Pomeranian hair fine enough for machine spinning. Trade forms are raw brushings, washed and carded batts, and finished yarn, which is either 100 percent dog undercoat or a blend with wool or silk.
chiengora.fabrics: Most chiengora is hand spun into knitting or crochet yarn and made into scarves, hats, mittens and shawls, often as keepsakes from a household pet. Blends with wool add elasticity and reduce shedding; silk adds strength and sheen. Plied yarns are preferred because they shed less than singles. Woven items are uncommon, though some weavers use dog-hair yarn as weft in blankets. The historical parallel, Coast Salish blankets woven with woolly-dog fiber, belongs to a distinct Indigenous tradition and should not be confused with modern pet yarn.
chiengora.quality: Good chiengora starts with clean, guard-hair-free undercoat brushed during shedding; stiff, straight hairs in the yarn signal poor sorting and will prickle. Wash quality matters: well-scoured yarn smells neutral even when damp. Plied, moderately twisted yarn sheds less than loosely spun singles. Because processing is small-scale, ask a mill or spinner about minimum fiber weight, blend options and whether batches are kept separate if you want your own dog's fiber back. Commercial sale of dog-hair products in the US raises unresolved questions under the Dog and Cat Protection Act, so most chiengora is custom spun rather than sold at retail.
pros: Uses fiber that would otherwise be discarded after grooming.
Medullated undercoat gives a warm, lofty, haloed yarn.
Keepsake yarn has personal value that commercial fiber cannot offer.
No animal is harmed when fiber is brushed out during natural shedding.
cons: Yarn sheds and can develop a wet-dog smell if not thoroughly washed.
Dog allergens are present in hair, and so-called hypoallergenic breeds are no exception.
Quality varies strongly by breed and collection, and quantities per dog are small.
Commercial sale of dog-hair products is legally uncertain in the US and banned in the EU for dog fur.
chiengora.impact: Chiengora is a waste-recovery craft: fiber comes from routine grooming of companion animals and needs no land, feed or animals raised for the purpose. Environmental inputs are limited to washing water, detergent and the energy of small-scale carding and spinning, and no life cycle data exist. Animal welfare concerns are minimal when fiber is brushed out during shedding. The main social issue is legal and ethical: the US Dog and Cat Protection Act and the EU ban on cat and dog fur address dog fur products, and how they apply to yarn from shed hair is not settled, so commercial sellers should get legal advice.
chiengora.care: Hand wash in lukewarm water, about 30 C, with a wool or pet-safe mild detergent, and rinse thoroughly, since residual skin oils cause odor. A vinegar rinse is sometimes used by spinners to reduce smell. Do not agitate or change water temperature abruptly, as the fiber can felt, especially in wool blends. Press out water in a towel and dry flat, away from heat. Do not tumble dry or iron directly; steam lightly if needed. Store clean and dry with a moth deterrent, because dog hair is keratin and attracts clothes moths and carpet beetles. Expect some shedding; plied yarns shed less.
faq: Can I make yarn from my dog's hair?

Yes, if your dog has a soft, reasonably long undercoat. Brush during shedding, keep the undercoat separate from guard hairs and debris, and store it dry. Several ounces are usually needed for a small project, and many spinners blend it with wool.

Properly washed yarn should not. Odor comes from skin oils and dander left in the fiber, so thorough scouring before spinning and a careful wash of the finished item are important. A lingering smell when damp suggests incomplete cleaning.
Is dog hair yarn safe for people with dog allergies?

Not necessarily. A 2012 study found the major dog allergen Can f 1 in hair and coat samples of all breeds tested, with higher levels in so-called hypoallergenic breeds. Washing may reduce allergen, but it has not been shown to remove it.
Is dog hair yarn warmer than wool?

Craft sources often say so, attributing warmth to the air-filled medulla of dog hair, but no standardized test supports a specific figure. Warmth in a finished item depends mostly on yarn thickness, spinning style and knit structure.
notable: A 2012 study found higher Can f 1 allergen levels in the hair and coats of so-called hypoallergenic dog breeds than in Labrador retrievers.
The medulla that makes dog hair lofty also makes the fiber less resistant to bending, one reason chiengora sheds.
In a five-breed study, only the finer Lhasa Apso and Pomeranian hair was slender enough for machine spinning.
